items.summary: Restored AD service account support for app deployment and desktop image application. This function is hidden by default and enabled via the Features:UamServiceAccounts feature flag for environments where domain policy restricts local admin or non-approved accounts.

items.title: Scripted Sequences (Preview):
items.summary: Concurrency balancer: Added a concurrency balancer option to the Run Scripted Sequence dialog for AVD, allowing admins to limit concurrent executions globally or per host pool to prevent overload in large environments. Task Worker deletion: Admins can now delete task workers directly from the Task Workers page, triggering a deletion signal to the endpoint worker, which removes itself from the device and reports back confirmation. Deleted workers are filterable via Show Deleted and must be redeployed if needed in future.

items.title: Intune Insights Update Ring reporting:
items.summary: For devices assigned to an Intune Update Ring, the ring's deferral period is now applied before Nerdio Manager's update-age countdown begins. For example, where Nerdio Manager is configured to mark devices Amber after 7 days and Red after 14 days, that countdown only starts once the deferral period has passed.

items.title: Cost & Efficiency Insights:
items.summary: User Cost Attribution show tags in use: The User Cost Attribution page now more clearly displays the specific Azure tags that are in use and in scope of the calculations on the page. User Cost Attribution TLS 1.3 support: User Cost Attribution now supports TLS 1.3 for secure data transmission. Operational Efficiency includes Intune scripts backup recommendations: Operational Efficiency recommendations now include an Intune recommendation to back up Intune scripts.

items.title: Search:
items.summary: Dedicated search results page: Pressing Enter in the global search now opens a dedicated, full-page results view (previously results appeared only in the dropdown), making it easier to browse all matches across users, sessions, apps, policies, and more. Custom tags: Where a set of resources in an Azure deployment has been tagged with a specific custom tag or tags, NME can now search by either the custom tag name or tag value to find all matching resources. Intune policies: NME search now supports searching for Intune policies directly from the global search bar. Approval requests: Approval requests can now be found directly from the global search bar, respecting permissions and working across all Intune tenants the user can access. When searching by user, admins can show requests created or reviewed by that user, with results opening the Approval Requests page with the filter already applied.

items.title: Refreshed Updates page:
items.summary: Refreshed the Updates page layout, now showing additional versions for rollback.

items.title: Least-privilege Azure custom role support (Preview):
items.summary: Nerdio Manager now supports running with a least-privilege custom Azure role instead of requiring Contributor access.

items.title: Granular RBAC permissions for secure variables:
items.summary: Secure variables now have a dedicated RBAC module with independent permission levels: Read Only , Manage , and Show Secret . Admins can grant view or management rights on secure variables separately from the ability to reveal plaintext values.

items.title: Console Connect Japan region support:
items.summary: Console Connect now supports the Japan region for data residency.

items.title: Egress method indicator:
items.summary: Host pool and individual session host pages now display the outbound network egress method in use (e.g., NAT Gateway, Azure Firewall, Default Outbound Access), with a warning indicator shown when a host or host pool relies on deprecated Default Outbound Access.

items.title: Azure Key Vault RBAC authorization model:
items.summary: New Nerdio Manager deployments now create key vaults using Azure's RBAC permission model. Existing environments using the access-policy model continue to work, with updated APIs keeping them supported.

items.title: REST API endpoints:
items.summary: Added the following: Full CRUD support for Scripted Action profiles. Full CRUD support for Scripted Action groups. A new endpoint to query a user's entitlements and assignments. Support for encryptionAtHost on the Desktop Image creation endpoint.

items.title: Azure NetApp Files Basic network features:
items.summary: The Basic network features option has been removed when creating or modifying volumes, as it has been deprecated by Microsoft effective July 2026 .

items.title: Intune:
items.summary: Policy read-only view mode: Fixed an issue where admins with read-only Intune permissions could not view policy details in NME. Policies can now be opened and navigated in read-only mode, including content, assignments, and settings. Antivirus Report: Reorganized the Antivirus Report page from large status buttons into standard tabs with count badges, improving visibility on 1920×1080 screens.

items.title: Applications:
items.summary: SCCM import path length: Shortened the temp directory name used during SCCM app exports to reduce path length, preventing import failures caused by exceeding the Windows 260-character path limit in some SCCM environments. Deployment policy status: Fixed an issue where UAM policy deployment to an Intune device could get stuck in a failed state indefinitely when the initial task worker deployment to the device had failed. WinGet uninstall all versions: Fixed an issue where not all installed versions of an application were removed when uninstalling via WinGet policy. All discrete versions are now removed using the WinGet --all flag.

items.title: Automations:
items.summary: Scripted sequences — Shell App binary extraction: Fixed an issue where zipped Shell App binaries were being extracted multiple times per deployment stage. Archives are now unzipped directly from cache once per installation, reducing the probability of deployment timeouts in scenarios with binary-heavy payloads. Cloning Scripted Actions: Resolved an issue where cloning a Scripted Action could fail.

items.title: Licensing for Citrix Platform Flex

items.title: Configurable inactivity timeout for console
items.summary: Full-access administrators can now configure the duration of inactivity on the Citrix Cloud console before administrators are automatically signed out. The configurable inactivity timeout ranges from 10 minutes to 12 hours, with a default of 60 minutes. For more information, see System and Connectivity Requirements .

items.title: Conditional Authentication enhancements
items.summary: Conditional Authentication now supports additional identity providers and policy conditions. For more information, see Conditional Authentication .

items.title: SAML using Entra ID for Guest and B2B identities
items.summary: Citrix Cloud now supports store authentication for guest and B2B user identities using Entra ID as a SAML provider. For more information, see SAML using Entra ID for Guest and B2B identities for store authentication .

items.title: Citrix DaaS MCP server is now available in preview
items.summary: Citrix DaaS MCP server is now available in preview Your Citrix DaaS Monitor dashboard shows 47 machines in a warning state. You open DaaS Director, click into a delivery group, drill into a machine, check the session, cross-reference the users’ connection failures. After several rounds of analysis of metrics and logs, you may have an answer. Now picture this instead: you type "Why are machines failing in the London delivery group?" into your AI assistant, and in seconds you get back the machines involved, the specific errors, session metrics, and which users are affected. No console switching. No manual correlation. That's what the Citrix DaaS MCP server makes possible. It connects your AI assistant directly to your on-premises DaaS Delivery Controller, so you can query your Citrix DaaS environment using plain language and get answers from live data. The same data Citrix DaaS Monitor uses, without navigating through multiple views to piece it together. It's now available in preview.   What you can ask Prompts you enter in your AI client run against your own Citrix DaaS environment, under your admin credentials, and return live data using the available MCP tools.   Troubleshoot a user's session"Show me the session performance metrics for user jane.doe. Also, check if she had any connection failures in the last 24 hours." Instead of navigating between session details, the user’s session performance metrics and failure logs in DaaS Director, you get all relevant details extracted and sent to your AI agent for a single response. Find machines that need attention"Which DaaS VDA machines are unregistered in the Finance delivery group? For any unregistered machines, show me their recent failures and troubleshoot why" Instead of finding affected machines and then triaging their issues, your AI agent can use the data retrieved for your environment and provide holistic analysis. Run ad-hoc data queries"Show me all sessions that had a logon duration over 60 seconds in the last 3 days, grouped by delivery group." Questions that would normally require writing OData queries or exporting data from DaaS Director can be answered in plain language. The AI client handles the query construction and returns structured results using the provided MCP tools. Spot capacity issues before they become outages"List the top 10 most-loaded multi-session machines. For the top 3, show me their resource usage trends." The server ranks machines by load, runs resource utilization analysis with anomaly detection, and flags saturation patterns. Capacity concerns surface before users start calling the help desk.   What data you can query The MCP server exposes 20 query capabilities across your Citrix DaaS environment: Site overview: Current connection failure counts by type, failed machine counts, connected session activity over the last hour, hypervisor connection details, and group policy configuration including settings and filters.  Delivery groups and machine catalogs: Search and filter by name, maintenance mode, enabled state, sharing kind, session support, allocation type, and provisioning type. Retrieve detailed configuration for any group or catalog.  VDA: Search by delivery group, catalog, agent version, OS type, tags, maintenance mode, power state, registration state, session state, and fault state. Resource utilization analysis with statistical profiling (mean, P95, max), anomaly detection, saturation pattern detection, and actionable recommendations. Load ranking for multi-session machines by effective load index.  Sessions: Search by user, machine, delivery group, catalog, session state, and applications in use. Real-time performance metrics within the last 2 hours. Logon duration breakdowns showing each logon phase with its duration and timing.  Users and endpoints: Active sessions by user (with machine name, DNS, IP, agent version), active users on a machine (with UPN, full name, domain), and endpoint device metrics for the connecting client within the last 2 hours.  Connection failures: Failed connection attempts by user (last 7 days) or transaction ID (last 90 days).  Custom OData queries: Run any query against the DaaS Monitor OData service in plain language, with automatic pagination for up to 10,000 rows. Built-in OData reference documentation helps the AI assistant navigate entity relationships and construct queries correctly. All 20 tools are read-only. The server queries data from your DaaS Delivery Controller. It does not create, modify, or delete anything.   Your data stays in your environmentThe Citrix DaaS MCP server runs locally on your Windows machine and communicates directly with your DaaS Delivery Controller over your network. When you ask a question: Your AI assistant determines what data it needs The MCP server queries your DaaS Delivery Controller Results come back to your AI assistant, which puts together a response Everything stays local. No data is sent to external services by the MCP server. Credentials are stored in Windows Credential Manager, protected by your Windows account, and never written to disk in plain text. The data you can access reflects the permissions of the administrator account you configure, i.e., if your account has read-only Delegated Admin access, that's what the server can see.  Getting started You need a Windows 11 machine with Node.js 18+ installed, network connectivity to your DaaS Delivery Controller, and a domain account with a Citrix DaaS administrator role. Your DaaS Local deployment must be version 2402 LTSR or later.  Setup takes under 5 minutes:  Download the bundle from the Citrix download page  Run the configuration command in PowerShell  Enter your DaaS Delivery Controller hostname and administrator credentials  The installer runs a self-test. If it passes, you're connected.  The MCP server works with any AI client that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standard. Claude Code has been validated and is configured automatically during setup. For other MCP clients, the installer generates a configuration block you can copy into your client's settings.  For detailed setup instructions, see the product documentation.  What's next This Preview release focuses on read-only monitoring and troubleshooting queries for on-premises environments. We're actively working on expanding coverage to cloud deployments and improved capabilities in future releases.  Download the MCP bundle today, connect it to your AI client, and try it against your own environment. We want to hear what questions you're asking and what use cases matter most to you!

items.title: Protecting automotive and manufacturing innovation without slowing down
items.summary: Why organizations need context-aware Citrix security  Today’s automotive and manufacturing ecosystems are powered by global collaboration. OEMs, Tier 1 suppliers, engineering service providers, software developers, and specialized contractors collaborate seamlessly across continents, organizations, and time zones. A single vehicle platform involves hundreds of enterprise partners and thousands of remote engineers contributing to design, simulation, validation, and production. While this collaborative model accelerates time-to-market, it also exposes organizations to significant risk.   As Kaspersky ICS CERT notes, “The current trend is supply chain attacks on automaker infrastructure via hacked contractor systems.”  This makes contractor access not only an operational requirement, but also a potential route into high-value systems and intellectual property.   This growing exposure raises a critical question: How can organizations give external partners access to sensitive operational tools without compromising the core intellectual property that defines their competitive advantage?  Why risk doesn't stop at authentication For many manufacturing leaders, Citrix DaaS environments have long served as the baseline standard for secure access. By centralizing sensitive CAD applications, PLM systems, and project files, virtualization minimizes the risk of endpoint data leaks. However, as workforce models become increasingly hybrid and distributed, traditional perimeter-based controls are reaching their limits.   Consider a common engineering workflow: an external development partner connects to a Citrix-hosted engineering environment. At logon, authentication succeeds, multi-factor authentication (MFA) is verified, and session access is granted. Traditional security controls stop here, but the security context is dynamic. During a long-running engineering session, the risk landscape can shift dramatically:  The user may switch from a secure corporate network to an unencrypted public Wi-Fi connection.  Endpoint security agents or firewall configurations on the device may fail or be manually disabled.  The device posture may degrade while sensitive intellectual property is still active on screen.  What’s at stake for automotive and manufacturing leaders Automotive and manufacturing organizations face a complex balancing act. They must enable frictionless partner and supplier collaboration while safeguarding critical enterprise assets including:  High-value intellectual property and CAD designs  Engineering and R&D simulation environments  Sensitive customer and supplier information  Security teams face a difficult choice:   Neither approach scales in today’s fast-paced market. A third zero trust approach uses adaptive, context-aware security to adjust access rights as risk changes during the session.  Zero trust requires visibility beyond authentication Identity is a crucial pillar of zero trust, but identity alone lacks the context required to evaluate session risk dynamically. Security teams need answers to ongoing operational questions:  Is the user’s endpoint compliant with organizational security policies?  Are active endpoint protection and local firewalls running properly?  Is the connection originating from an approved network and geographic location?  Has the security posture of the endpoint changed since the session began?  For sessions that stay open for hours, these questions are just as vital midway through a shift as they were at logon. Without continuous validation, a widening gap emerges between policy intent and actual risk.  Bring contextual security to Citrix DaaS with deviceTrust Citrix deviceTRUST bridges this gap by extending the standard Citrix DaaS security model with real-time contextual access controls operating inside active user sessions. Rather than relying solely on a single decision made during initial authentication, Citrix deviceTRUST continuously monitors context signals from the endpoint and network environment. When contextual conditions change, access permissions adapt dynamically without disrupting user productivity.  Citrix deviceTRUST key capabilities Continuous posture assessment: Tracks OS health, firewall/antivirus status, network environment, and geolocation throughout the session.  Dynamic policy enforcement: Automatically adjusts session capabilities based on live risk levels.  Seamless integration: Integrates natively into existing Citrix architectures and communication channels without requiring complex infrastructural overhauls.  Real-world automotive and manufacturing use cases To demonstrate how context-aware security operates in dynamic production and engineering environments, consider the following real-world implementation scenarios:  Controlled external engineer access (TISAX-certified locations and managed devices) Scenario: External engineering service providers and Tier 1 partner teams require access to central design platforms and PLM tools.  Contextual policy requirements: Access is permitted exclusively when external engineers use certified, corporate-managed endpoints connecting directly from TISAX (Trusted Information Security Assessment Exchange) -certified physical locations.  Real-time enforcement: Citrix deviceTRUST continuously validates device management status and location compliance. If an unmanaged endpoint or non-certified location is detected, even after successful login, access permissions are dynamically restricted or terminated.  Geofenced access to confidential data Scenario: Access to confidential R&D projects, next-generation platform blueprints, and proprietary test data demands strict perimeter controls.  Contextual policy requirements: Access to confidential development data strictly mandates physical presence within the corporate campus network boundaries.  Real-time enforcement: Using continuous geofencing verification, Citrix deviceTRUST monitors connection parameters during active sessions. If a user attempts to open confidential R&D files from outside authorized corporate campus locations, access to sensitive datasets is immediately blocked.  4 practical next steps to elevate your Citrix DaaS security  To identify where contextual security could strengthen a Citrix DaaS environment, begin with these five steps:  Audit high-value assets: Identify the core application suites, source code repositories, and CAD/PLM databases containing your most critical IP.  Evaluate external access points: Map out how suppliers, contractors, and offshore engineering teams currently access these environments.  Compare logon controls vs. session controls: Assess which security controls operate strictly at initial authentication versus those enforced continuously during an active session.  Deploy a targeted Citrix deviceTRUST pilot: Choose one high-risk, high-value scenario (such as contractor drive mapping restriction) to explore real-time policy enforcement.  Continuous context checks help automotive and manufacturing organizations respond when device, network, or location risk changes during a Citrix DaaS session. External partners retain the access needed for engineering work, while intellectual property remains protected as conditions change.

items.title: Protecting NetScaler Management Access from PHP CVE-2026-109618 & CVE 2026-109619
items.summary: Immediate mitigation guidance for NetScaler customers By NetScaler Product Security  NetScaler is impacted by two PHP memory safety vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) because the NetScaler Management Portal uses PHP.  As recommended in NetScaler’s Secure Deployment Guide, management interfaces must be logically or physically isolated from data traffic, completely blocked from the Internet, and restricted via ACLs to trusted administrative subnets only.   Customers should immediately restrict access to NetScaler management interfaces to trusted, limited networks. This step reduces exposure by ensuring that only authorized administrative systems and users can access the management GUI and APIs.  Citrix has released fixes to address these two PHP memory safety vulnerabilities for all supported NetScaler software versions. NetScaler 14.1 and 13.1 builds containing the fix are now available.  About the vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities in PHP that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code in the context of the affected PHP process. Both vulnerabilities are rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0.  CVE-2026-109618 involves memory corruption when PHP handles an out-of-memory condition during request processing.  CVE-2026-109619 involves stale request state that can persist after memory is released and can then be reused by a subsequent request.   What is affected? The following NetScaler management interfaces use the PHP-based management access and are affected:  NSIP GUI — the NetScaler IP management interface.  SNIP with management access enabled — any Subnet IP configured to permit management access.  Cluster IP GUI — when NetScaler is deployed as a cluster.  Customers should review every  IP address that permits GUI or API-based management and verify that it is not broadly reachable.  All supported NetScaler software versions are impacted. NetScaler Console (Service and on premises) and NetScaler SVM are not impacted by this vulnerability.   Recommended immediate mitigation Restrict GUI & API access on the NSIP, management-enabled SNIPs and the Cluster IP to trusted administrative hosts or narrowly scoped management networks. Wherever possible, keep management interfaces on isolated networks that are not Internet-facing and use jump hosts or tightly scoped ACLs to limit administrative access.  Example: allow NSIP GUI access only from a trusted host or network The following example permits HTTP and HTTPS management access to the NSIP from a trusted administrative source, then denies all other sources:  add ns acl allow-adm-80 ALLOW -srcIP = <Console_IP/Trusted_IP> -destIP = <NSIP> -destPort = 80 -protocol TCP -priority 1  add ns acl allow-adm-443 ALLOW -srcIP = <Console_IP/Trusted_IP> -destIP = <NSIP> -destPort = 443 -protocol TCP -priority 2  add ns acl deny-rest-all-80 DENY -destIP = <NSIP> -destPort = 80 -protocol TCP -priority 3  add ns acl deny-rest-all-443 DENY -destIP = <NSIP> -destPort = 443 -protocol TCP -priority 4  apply ns acls  Replace the placeholders with the appropriate addresses for your environment. To permit a subnet or a trusted host on NetScaler using the CLI, you must add an ALLOW rule using an IP address range for subnets:  add ns acl <ACL_Name> ALLOW -srcIP <Start_IP>-<End_IP> -priority <Number>  Important implementation considerations Preserve NetScaler Console access so that licensing and centralized management continue to work.  Validate the ACLs and confirm that authorized administrators retain access before ending the session.  Account for required management, monitoring, automation, DNS, authentication, and health-monitor traffic before applying DENY rules.  Use caution when restricting a SNIP or VIP because it can also carry application traffic. Scope ACLs specifically to management protocols and ports to avoid service disruption.  Apply equivalent restrictions to every management-enabled IP, including the Cluster IP in cluster deployments.  Maintain an approved recovery path, such as console access, in case an ACL unintentionally blocks administration.  For detailed guidance, see How to Restrict NetScaler Management Interfaces with ACLs (CTX228148).    Common customer questions Will Citrix provide WAF signatures for backend applications running PHP? Yes, WAF signature (v186) has been released. Please refer to this blog   Will Citrix provide WAF signatures to protect affected NetScaler management interfaces (NSIP GUI, SNIP, and Cluster IP) from CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619? We are developing signatures to protect NetScaler from these vulnerabilities and will update this blog when they are available.   Last updated on: October 27, 2026 (Pacific Daylight Time)

items.title: NetScaler WAF Signatures Update v186
items.summary: NetScaler has released a new version of its integrated Web App Firewall signatures to help customers mitigate several CVEs with varying CVSS scores.    CVE‑2026‑109618: is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in PHP’s handling of out-of-memory errors. PHP uses longjmp() to abort a request after memory exhaustion; in some execution paths, this can leave request memory uninitialized. During cleanup, PHP may read or branch on that memory, allowing a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code by sending crafted web requests that trigger the condition.  CVE2026-109619: is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in PHP caused by improper cleanup after a fatal error. PHP can leave global state pointing to freed memory, and a subsequent request may read or branch on that stale memory. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this use-after-free condition with crafted web requests to execute arbitrary code as the affected PHP worker. Customers should upgrade immediately to PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, or 8.5.12, as applicable.  Signatures included in v186 Following is a list of signature rules, CVE IDs, and its description.   Signature rule  CVE ID  Description  998061  CVE-2026-109619  WEB-MISC PHP Multiple Versions - Global Stale State Vulnerability upload_progress (CVE-2026-109619)  998062  CVE-2026-109618  WEB-MISC PHP Multiple Versions - Multipart Part With Excessive Headers Memory Exhaustion (CVE-2026-109618)   NetScaler customers can quickly import the above signatures to help reduce risk and lower exposure associated with these vulnerabilities. Signatures are compatible with NetScaler (formerly Citrix ADC) software versions 12.1, 13.0, 13.1, and 14.1.   NOTE: Software versions 11.1 and 12.0 are end of life, and you should consider upgrading for continued support. Learn more about the NetScaler software release lifecycle.    If you are already using NetScaler Web App Firewall with the signature auto-update feature enabled, verify that your signature file version is 183 or later and then follow these steps.   Search your signatures for <number>   Select the results with ID    Choose “Enable Rules” and click OK   NetScaler WAF Best Practices  NetScaler recommends that WAF users always download the latest signature version, enable signature auto-update, and subscribe to receive signature alert notifications. NetScaler will continue to monitor this dynamic situation and provide updates as new mitigations become available.   Handling false positives  If app availability is affected by false positives that result from the above mitigation policies, relaxations can be applied. NetScaler recommends the following modifications to the policy.   Modifications to NetScaler Web App Firewall Policy:   add policy patset exception_list   # (Example: bind policy patset exception_list “/exception_url”)    Prepend the existing WAF policy with:   HTTP.REQ.URL.CONTAINS_ANY(“exception_list”).NOT   # (Example:  set appfw policy my_WAF_policy q^HTTP.REQ.URL.CONTAINS_ANY(“exception_list”).NOT && <existing rule>^   NOTE: Any endpoint covered by the exception_list may expose the associated assets to risks    Additional Information  NetScaler Web App Firewall benefits from a single code base across all its form-factors (physical, virtual, bare-metal, and containers). This signature update applies to all form factors and deployment models of NetScaler Web App Firewall.   Learn more about NetScaler Web App Firewall. Read our alert articles and bot signature articles to learn more about NetScaler WAF signatures and find out how you can receive signature alert notifications.   Please join the NetScaler Community today and engage with your peers to learn more about how they are protecting their businesses with NetScaler WAF.

items.title: How Do I: Validate a NetScaler upgrade and confirm it succeeded?
items.summary: A practical post-upgrade validation guide for NetScaler ADC administrators   The install finished and the appliance came back up. Is the upgrade done? A clean reboot does not prove that every node runs the intended build, that the configuration and certificates came through intact, that HA or cluster synchronization is restored, or that users can still sign in and complete transactions. This article gives NetScaler administrators a repeatable, three-stage validation approach to confirm all of that quickly and with evidence, so you can close the change with confidence and a clean baseline for the next one.  What a “successful upgrade” looks like Platform: Every appliance or node is reachable and reports the approved target release and build.  Configuration: The saved and running configuration, certificates, routes, policies, and customizations are present and valid.  Availability: Virtual servers, services, service groups, and monitors are in their expected states.  Resiliency: HA or cluster health is restored, including synchronization, propagation, and failover behavior.  Function: Representative user journeys and application transactions succeed end to end.  Operations: Licensing, logging, monitoring, backups, and management connectivity work normally.  Stability: No unexplained increase appears in errors, resource use, latency, resets, or support alarms during the observation window.  Prerequisites before starting upgrade validation Upgrade completion confirmed: Verify that the upgrade procedure has completed on the intended appliance, HA pair, or cluster nodes, including required reboots and return of management access.  Target build known: Keep the approved target release and build details available so the post-upgrade software version can be verified on every upgraded node.  Pre-upgrade baseline available: Ensure the pre-upgrade inventory, configuration snapshot, application list, traffic metrics, and known exceptions are available for comparison.  Validation access ready: Confirm administrator access to the GUI, CLI, console or out-of-band path, monitoring tools, NetScaler Console, and relevant log locations.  Application test scope identified: Confirm the critical applications, DNS names, authentication flows, owner contacts, and representative transactions that must be validated after the upgrade.  Observation and escalation plan defined: Agree on the post-upgrade observation window, evidence requirements, issue owner, escalation path, and criteria for declaring the upgrade successful or requiring remediation.  Use a three-stage validation approach Run validation in three stages. First, perform an immediate platform check after each reboot. Next, complete functional and resiliency tests before closing the change. Finally, maintain a stability watch long enough to cover normal traffic patterns and scheduled integrations. This sequence creates fast feedback while avoiding a premature declaration of success.     Stage 1: Immediate platform checks 1.1 Confirm the appliance is on the intended build Log on through the management path and confirm CLI and GUI access.  Verify the reported NetScaler release and build against the approved change record.  For HA pairs and clusters, confirm that every node reaches the same intended software version before normal operations resume.  Confirm the appliance completed its reboot and that the system time, time zone, and NTP synchronization are correct.  Applicable CLI checks:  show ns version  show ns ip  show ntp status  1.2 Check system health and capacity from dashboard Review CPU, memory, packet-engine utilization, interface status, throughput, and connection counts for unexpected changes from the pre-upgrade baseline.      Confirm that /var and /flash have healthy free space after installation files, crash files, and temporary artifacts are accounted for.  Inspect recent system events and the relevant newnslog, ns.log, and messages files for boot failures, repeated restarts, hardware errors, license errors, configuration parsing failures, or feature initialization problems.  Confirm management services, DNS resolution, NTP, SNMP, syslog, call-home, and NetScaler Console connectivity where used.  Record any warning that is new after the upgrade, assign an owner, and determine whether it affects the success decision.  Applicable CLI checks:  stat system show interface show ns ip shell #df -h /var /flash #tail -n 100 /var/log/ns.log #tail -n 100 /var/log/messages 1.3 Validate configuration integrity Confirm that the running configuration loaded without errors and matches the approved post-upgrade configuration.  Compare key objects with the pre-upgrade inventory: NSIP, SNIPs, VIPs, VLANs, routes, DNS settings, virtual servers, services, service groups, monitors, policies, profiles, authentication objects, and bindings.  Verify that SSL certificates, certificate chains, keys, and bindings are present, valid, and not nearing expiry.  Reapply and validate supported customizations that were intentionally removed before the upgrade. Pay particular attention to customized files under /etc and to any HTTPD or SSHD overrides.  Save the validated configuration and create a fresh post-upgrade backup after the environment is stable.  Applicable CLI checks:  show ns runningConfig  diff ns config <pre-upgrade-config-file> <post-upgrade-config-file>  show ssl certKey  After validation: save ns config  Optional backup: create system backup <backup-name> -level full  1.4 Confirm licensing and feature availability Verify that the appliance is licensed as designed and that all required editions, bandwidth entitlements, and features remain available. Treat any unexpected fallback, expiry, or feature unavailability as a release-blocking issue. For pooled or License Activation Service (LAS) deployments, also confirm license-server connectivity and compatibility. NetScaler documentation notes that file-based licensing reached end of life on April 15, 2026, so current deployments should validate their supported LAS-based licensing path and compatible versions.  Applicable CLI check:  show ns license  Stage 2: Functional and resiliency validation 2.1 Confirm object and monitor states Confirm that production virtual servers are UP, or in another documented expected state.    Confirm that bound services and service-group members are UP and that monitor results are consistent with backend health.    Review disabled or out-of-service objects against the pre-upgrade baseline so that intentional states are not mistaken for failures.  Check persistence, spillover, load-balancing methods, content switching, responder, rewrite, caching, compression, and AppQoE behavior where those features are deployed.  Applicable CLI checks:  show lb vserver  show lb vserver <vserver-name>  show service  show serviceGroup  show lb monitor  2.2 Run representative end-to-end transactions Test each critical application through the same DNS name, protocol, network path, and authentication flow used by clients.  Validate a small set of high-value user journeys—for example, sign-in, application launch, API call, file transfer, or transaction completion—not only the landing page.  Test HTTP and HTTPS behavior, redirects, headers, cookies, persistence, and expected TLS negotiation.  Where applicable, test NetScaler Gateway, AAA, nFactor, SAML, OAuth, LDAP, RADIUS, certificate authentication, and session policies.  For GSLB, confirm site, service, and domain status; validate DNS responses and verify that synchronization behaves as designed.  Compare response time, error rate, reset rate, and throughput with the pre-upgrade baseline.  Applicable CLI checks (use only for deployed features):  show cs vserver  show vpn vserver  show authentication vserver  show gslb vserver  show gslb service  show gslb domain  2.3 Validate resiliency 2.3.1 High availability pairs   Confirm both nodes are UP, on the same release and build, and in the intended primary/secondary roles.    Verify HA synchronization, command propagation, state synchronization, connection mirroring, and persistence synchronization are restored as applicable.  Confirm there are no unintended STAYPRIMARY or STAYSECONDARY settings.    Compare the configuration on both nodes and verify expected synchronized files and certificates.   Applicable CLI checks:  show ha node  show ha node -summary  show ns version  Note: Run failover commands only within an approved change plan; verify state and application traffic before and after the controlled failover.  2.3.2 Clusters Confirm every cluster node is UP and running the same software version.  Verify cluster instance status, node health, backplane connectivity, traffic distribution, and configuration propagation.  Do not make configuration changes through the cluster IP while version mismatch has disabled propagation.  After all nodes are upgraded, confirm propagation is enabled and validate a controlled node-level traffic test or failover scenario.  Applicable CLI checks:  show cluster instance  show cluster node  show cluster syncFailures  Corrective action when approved: force cluster sync  2.4 Complete the post-upgrade acceptance checklist   Area  Minimum acceptance evidence  Status  Build and access  Approved build on every node; GUI, CLI, and management reachability confirmed  Pass / Review  System health  No critical boot, hardware, disk, resource, or recurring log errors  Pass / Review  Configuration  Key objects, settings, certificates, policies, and customizations verified  Pass / Review  Licensing  Expected license state, capacity, and licensed features available  Pass / Review  Application delivery  Critical virtual servers, services, service groups, and monitors in expected states  Pass / Review  User journeys  Representative transactions complete successfully through production paths  Pass / Review  HA or cluster  All nodes healthy; synchronization or propagation restored; resiliency test completed  Pass / Review  Observability  SNMP, syslog, analytics, alerting, and Console data are current  Pass / Review  Stability  Metrics remain within agreed baseline during the observation window  Pass / Review  Closeout  Configuration saved, post-upgrade backup captured, evidence attached, stakeholders informed  Pass / Review    Stage 3: Stability watch and change closure 3.1 Monitor stability during the observation window Choose an observation window that covers meaningful traffic, integrations, and scheduled jobs. During that period, compare current behavior with the pre-upgrade baseline. Focus on availability, latency, throughput, connection counts, HTTP response codes, SSL errors, authentication failures, monitor flaps, packet drops, resets, CPU, memory, and disk growth. A stable trend is stronger evidence than a single successful test.  3.2 Capture the recommended evidence package Target release and build for every node  Upgrade completion record and reboot time  Before-and-after configuration or inventory comparison  HA or cluster status and resiliency-test result  Application test results and owner confirmation  Monitoring snapshots for the agreed observation window  Exceptions, business impact, owner, and planned resolution  Post-upgrade backup location and change-record closure  3.3 Confirm success and close the change Decision rule: Declare the upgrade successful when all release-blocking checks pass, expected redundancy is restored, critical user journeys succeed, and the stability window shows no material regression. Document and accept only low-risk exceptions with a named owner and target date.  If a check needs attention A failed check is useful because it narrows the next action. Keep the environment controlled, preserve evidence, and work from the smallest affected layer outward:  Confirm management access, the active release and build, and the current node role.  Review configuration-load messages and compare the affected object with the pre-upgrade configuration.  Check service and monitor states, then test backend reachability directly from the appliance.  Review newnslog, ns.log, and messages for the time of the upgrade and the failed test.  For HA or cluster issues, first eliminate version mismatch and restore synchronization or propagation before making routine configuration changes.  For license-related symptoms, verify entitlement, expiry, License Activation Service or license-server reachability, and version compatibility.  If escalation is required, provide configuration files from the relevant appliances, logs, timestamps, symptoms, topology, and the exact tests already completed.  Useful troubleshooting CLI checks:  show ns version  show ns runningConfig  show lb vserver <vserver-name>  show service <service-name>  show serviceGroup <service-group-name>  show ha node  show cluster node   Conclusion NetScaler upgrades are easiest to approve when success is defined before the maintenance begins and verified with consistent evidence afterward. By confirming the build, platform health, configuration, licensing, application behavior, resiliency, and stability, teams can return the environment to service with confidence and carry a clean baseline into the next change.    What's next?This article is part of our NetScaler upgrade series. For help with upgrade execution, explore these related guides: How Do I: Perform zero-downtime NetScaler upgrades using ISSU? Learn how to keep established connections alive during an HA upgrade. How Do I: Plan and Execute NetScaler Upgrades with Console Upgrade Jobs? Learn how to select instances, check readiness, schedule upgrades, and review results from one centralized workflow. Got stuck or hit something unexpected in your environment? Drop a comment, and we will help work through it. items.title: How Do I: Plan and Execute NetScaler Upgrades with Console Upgrade Jobs?
items.summary: A practical, step-by-step guide for NetScaler administrators upgrading standalone, HA, and cluster deployments from NetScaler Console   Introduction to Upgrade Jobs Upgrading one NetScaler is routine. Upgrading forty, across HA pairs, clusters, and regions, during a single maintenance window is where things go wrong: an SSH session drops, a node runs out of disk space halfway through, or nobody can say which appliances actually finished. If your upgrade "runbook" is a spreadsheet and a stack of terminal windows, this article is for you.  Upgrade Jobs in NetScaler Console replaces that manual process with one guided workflow. You pick the instances, choose the software image, run built-in readiness checks, capture before-and-after state with your own commands, and schedule the job. Then you review results for every instance in one place. By the end of this walkthrough, you'll have created, validated, and scheduled an Upgrade Job, and you'll know what to do if it fails.  Centralized orchestration: Manage upgrade activity from NetScaler Console instead of running a separate upgrade manually on each appliance.  Validation before change: Use built-in readiness checks and optional custom commands to identify blockers and capture a baseline before execution.  Controlled execution: Run immediately or schedule later, choose image-upload timing, and use HA-specific options where applicable.  Evidence and reporting: Review execution history and optionally receive execution reports through configured notification channels.   Key guardrail  NetScaler Console service supports up to 100 concurrent upgrade threads. Treat this as a service limit, not a recommended default batch size.   Upgrade Jobs use cases at a glance NetScaler Console provides the following Upgrade Job workflows:  Upgrade NetScaler for standalone appliances, HA pairs, and clusters  Upgrade NetScaler SDX  Upgrade NetScaler BLX  Upgrade Autoscale Group  Configure HA Pair  Convert HA Pair to a 2-Node Cluster    Why does this matter? Manual, appliance-by-appliance upgrades create three recurring problems:  Inconsistent readiness checks. Whether disk space, HA state, or policy compatibility gets checked depends on who runs the upgrade that night.  No single record. Progress and evidence are scattered across sessions and devices, so it's hard to prove what changed, or to spot what didn't.  Poor scaling. Every extra appliance adds more manual steps, more chances for error, and a longer maintenance window.  Upgrade Jobs gives you one repeatable control point. Built-in pre-validation flags blocking issues before the window opens, custom commands capture a before-and-after baseline, and per-instance job status and execution history give you an audit trail for the change record. Upgrade Jobs supports standalone, HA, and cluster deployments, plus SDX, BLX, and Autoscale groups.    Prerequisites Before you create an Upgrade Job, make sure you have:  NetScaler Console service access, with a role that has permission to create and run Upgrade Jobs [Add exact role/permission name]  Target instances already managed by NetScaler Console and reachable over SSH  The target software image downloaded and available, either on your workstation or in the Console file browser  Supported versions: source build [Add minimum] → target build [Add target]. Review the release notes for known issues.  An approved maintenance window, with the time zone recorded  All readiness gates in the next section confirmed (licensing, disk, customizations, policy compatibility, HA state, and recovery assets)    Upgrade Strategy and Operational Planning Upgrade Jobs handles execution, but a successful upgrade starts with planning. Work through these five steps before you open the wizard. Skip ahead to How to create an Upgrade Job if your planning is already done.  1. Readiness gates Licensing: Confirm that the target release and entitlement model are compatible, including any License Activation Service requirements.  Disk and hardware health: Resolve insufficient capacity and hardware warnings before execution.  Configuration customizations: Back up custom files, especially changes under /etc, and document how they will be restored.  Policy compatibility: Use NSPEPI to identify and convert supported classic policies before moving to releases that no longer support them.  HA state: Clear STAYPRIMARY or STAYSECONDARY conditions and confirm healthy synchronization before the maintenance window.  Recovery assets: Secure the current build, configuration backup, licenses, certificates, custom files, and console or out-of-band access details.  2. Design the maintenance window and recovery plan For production upgrades, use an approved window with the time zone recorded. Include time for image transfer, validation, reboots, topology synchronization, application checks, and a recovery buffer.  Freeze point: Stop nonessential configuration changes so that backups and validation represent the state being upgraded.  Pre-check point: Complete validation early enough to remediate failures before the maintenance window starts.  Execution point: Begin while sufficient engineering, operations, and application-owner coverage remains available.  Decision point: Define the latest time to continue to the next node or wave. Pause when service checks remain incomplete rather than consuming the recovery buffer.  Recovery is not a universal one-click downgrade Rollback is a pre-engineered recovery procedure, not a universal one-click downgrade. Define triggers such as loss of access, persistent topology instability, service failure, or insufficient time. If triggered, stop later waves, stabilize traffic, restore the supported state, rerun health checks, and retain logs and validation evidence.  3. Use topology-aware sequencing High-availability pairs For HA pairs, use secondary-first execution: verify roles and health, upgrade the secondary, confirm recovery, transition traffic, upgrade the remaining node, and validate synchronization, services, and controlled failover. Keep any mixed-version period brief.  Clusters and Autoscale groups For clusters, validate capacity, hardware, connectivity, customizations, and redundancy on every node. For Autoscale groups, align graceful upgrade and connection draining with minimum capacity, health probes, scaling policy, and expected traffic.  4. Run large-scale upgrades in controlled waves Although NetScaler Console service supports up to 100 concurrent upgrade threads, use smaller batches based on redundancy, bandwidth, monitoring capacity, shared dependencies, and recovery staffing.  Wave  Typical scope  Purpose  Exit criteria  0 — Lab  Representative nonproduction appliances  Validate image, compatibility, automation, and recovery  Upgrade and recovery rehearsal pass with no unresolved blockers  1 — Canary  Small, low-risk production subset  Expose production-only dependencies with limited impact  Service and telemetry remain stable through the observation period  2 — Limited rollout  One region or application group  Validate repeatability and operational capacity  Error rate, latency, topology state, and support signals stay within thresholds  3 — Broad rollout  Remaining fleet in bounded batches  Complete deployment without saturating Console, network, or staff  Each batch closes cleanly before the next begins    Scale controls Separate failure domains so that one wave cannot remove all redundant capacity.  Use homogeneous batches with similar hardware, current builds, and configurations.  Define stop rules for failed service checks, excessive failure rate, or execution duration that threatens the recovery buffer.  Avoid overlapping upgrade or configuration jobs that target the same appliance or shared dependency.  5. Execute, validate, and close the upgrade Business reason, target build, scope, and maintenance window are approved.  Release notes, known issues, platform support, licensing, and policy compatibility are reviewed.  Instances are grouped by topology, dependency, criticality, and failure domain.  Disk, hardware, customization, connectivity, and HA or cluster checks have passed.  Backups, images, certificates, licenses, custom files, and recovery access are secured.  Canary scope, batch sizes, observation periods, exit criteria, and stop thresholds are documented.  Per-instance status is monitored; a failed upgrade does not automatically trigger the next wave.  Management access, interfaces, routes, certificates, authentication, persistence, virtual servers, services, topology health, and representative application transactions are validated.  Execution history, custom-script output, post-change evidence, and any recovery actions are retained with the change record.   Step-by-step: Create and run an Upgrade Job The documented workflow begins in NetScaler Console under Infrastructure > Upgrade Jobs. Select Create Job to open the maintenance-job wizard.  Step 1. Open Upgrade JobsSign in to NetScaler Console, navigate to Infrastructure > Upgrade Jobs, and select Create Job.    Figure 1. Upgrade Jobs page (Infrastructure > Upgrade Jobs) in NetScaler Console, showing the Create Job option.    Step 2. Choose the taskSelect Upgrade NetScaler (Standalone/High-Availability/Cluster). For SDX, BLX, or Autoscale, choose the matching task.    Figure 2. Task selection in the Create Maintenance Job wizard, including Upgrade NetScaler (Standalone/High-Availability/Cluster) and the SDX, BLX, and Autoscale upgrade tasks.    Step 3. Name the job and add instancesEnter a Job Name and add the target instances.  HA pair: add the primary instance.  Cluster: add the cluster IP address.      Figure 3. Entering the job name and adding target instances: the primary instance for HA pairs, or the cluster IP address for clusters.     Figure 4. The Add Instances dialog, filtered to instances in the Up state. Select the target instances and click OK to add them to the Upgrade Job.  Step 4. Select the software imageChoose Local to upload from the administrator workstation, or Appliance to use an image already available through the Console file browser. Optionally, enable skip upload if the image is already present and clean up the image after a successful upgrade   Step 5. Run pre-upgrade validationReview failed instances and resolve or remove them before continuing. For a cluster IP, the documented workflow performs pre-validation only on the specified instance, so validate the remaining cluster nodes separately.    Figure 5. Pre-upgrade validation results per instance, showing passed, warning, and critical (blocking) outcomes to resolve before continuing.   Step 6. Add optional custom scriptsType commands in the GUI or import them from a file. They run before and after the upgrade so you can compare state. Example baseline set:  show ns version  show interface  show ha node  show lb vserver  show service  show route  stat system    Step 7. Schedule and create the jobChoose Upgrade now or Schedule later, and set the execution date and start time.   Figure 6. Schedule Task settings for the Upgrade Job Then set image-upload timing, enable the backup and configuration-save options, enable ISSU for HA pairs where appropriate, and configure execution-report notifications. Select Create Job.  Figure 7. Create Job settings for image-upload timing, backup and configuration-save options, ISSU HA upgrade options, execution-report notifications  Step 8. Monitor and VerifyTrack per-instance status in the job's execution history. After the upgrade, confirm the build and topology health:  show ns version  show ha node  show cluster node    If something breaks Pre-validation shows Critical for disk space on /var or /flash: Clear old images, crash files, and core dumps, then rerun validation.  SSH connectivity check fails: Confirm Console can reach the instance, that the credentials and profile are current, and that host trust is valid.  NSPEPI check fails: Convert the classic policies with NSPEPI before upgrading to a release that no longer supports them.  HA configuration check fails: Clear STAYPRIMARY or STAYSECONDARY settings and confirm both nodes are synchronized (show ha node).  Image upload fails or stalls: Check bandwidth and free space, or switch to the Appliance option with a pre-staged image.  Job fails on one instance in a batch: Don't start the next wave. Review that instance's execution history and custom-script output, compare the output with the baseline, and fix the problem before resuming.  Still stuck? Collect the job execution history, custom-script output, and show techsupport from the affected appliance, then open a support case.   Upgrade Jobs use cases 1. Upgrade NetScaler (Standalone/HA/Cluster) Use for standalone appliances, HA pairs, and clusters. The job combines instance and image selection, readiness checks, optional pre/post commands, scheduling, backup, and reporting. Select the primary instance for HA; for clusters, use the cluster IP and verify readiness on every node.  2. Upgrade NetScaler SDX Use the dedicated job for managed NetScaler SDX platforms. Confirm image compatibility, connectivity, storage, hosted-instance impact, and recovery readiness. Upgrade multiple appliances in controlled batches and verify platform and hosted-instance health after each batch.  3. Upgrade NetScaler BLX Use for NetScaler BLX instances on supported Linux hosts. Validate both BLX service health and host prerequisites, capture a pre-upgrade baseline, then compare version, interfaces, services, routing, and application-path results after the upgrade.  4. Upgrade Autoscale Group Use when the entire Autoscale group is in scope. Coordinate member upgrades with graceful connection draining, minimum safe capacity, scaling policies, health probes, and expected traffic; verify capacity and service health throughout.  5. Configure HA Pair Use to form an HA pair from two compatible instances. Confirm reachability, software and feature alignment, authoritative configuration, and recovery access. Use Independent Network Configuration when node-specific network settings are required, then verify roles, synchronization, propagation, and failover.  6. Convert HA Pair to 2-Node Cluster Use to convert an existing two-node HA deployment into a two-node cluster. Provide node IDs, cluster IP, cluster ID, and backplane details; validate compatibility, connectivity, traffic impact, backups, and recovery. After conversion, verify membership, synchronization, cluster-IP reachability, backplane health, traffic distribution, and application services.   Validation and custom scripts Validation is the main control point that separates a repeatable Upgrade Job from a simple software installation. The Console performs built-in checks, and the custom-scripts step lets administrators compare environment-specific state before and after the change.  Built-in pre-upgrade validation Check  Purpose  Disk space on /var  Confirms sufficient capacity for image extraction and installation.  Disk space on /flash  Checks minimum free space for required system operations.  NSPEPI configuration  Detects unsupported or invalid policy configuration.  HA configuration  Verifies HA role and state consistency.  SSH connectivity  Confirms accessibility, trust validation, and connectivity to target devices.  Matching ns.conf for downgrade  Checks for a compatible configuration file for downgrade scenarios.  Result categories: Critical blocks the upgrade; Warning and Advisory permit continuation with administrator approval.  Custom scripts before and after upgrade Custom scripts are optional commands entered directly in the GUI or imported from a file. They are useful for comparing state before and after an upgrade, including software version, interfaces, HA nodes, virtual servers, services, statistics, and dynamic routes.  Recommended pattern: run the commands before the upgrade to capture a baseline, stop on a critical failure, rerun after each node or wave, compare results, and continue only when the agreed criteria pass.   Why Upgrade Jobs improve on traditional upgrades Area  Traditional upgrade  Upgrade Jobs  Execution model  Administrator performs appliance-by-appliance actions.  Central wizard selects instances, image, validation, schedule, and reporting.  Pre-change controls  Readiness checks depend on the local runbook and operator discipline.  Built-in pre-validation identifies blocking, warning, and advisory conditions.  Consistency  Steps and evidence can vary between operators and maintenance windows.  The same workflow and options can be reused across managed instances.  HA operations  Failover sequencing and timing are coordinated manually.  HA-aware sequencing, two-stage scheduling, and optional ISSU controls are integrated.  Validation  Pre/post checks are run separately and compared manually.  Custom commands can be captured in the job to check state before and after upgrade.  Scheduling  Execution is tied to the administrator session and manual timing.  Jobs can run immediately or at a defined execution date and start time.  Scale and visibility  Progress is tracked across separate sessions and devices.  Per-instance job status, execution history, and reports provide a centralized operational record.  Image and cleanup  Image upload and cleanup are separate manual steps.  Upload timing, skip-if-present, and cleanup-after-success options are part of the workflow.   Practical operating guidance Use staged waves: start in a lab, move to a small canary, expand to a limited group, and proceed to broad rollout only after exit criteria pass.  Size concurrency conservatively: base batch size on redundancy, image-transfer bandwidth, monitoring capacity, and recovery staffing, not only the platform maximum.  Protect recovery options: enable the documented backup and configuration-save controls, retain required images and access methods, and define the latest safe recovery decision time.  Validate every cluster node: when the workflow validates only the instance represented by the cluster IP, run equivalent checks for the remaining nodes before execution.  Retain evidence: keep job results, custom-script output, execution history, and representative application checks with the change record.   What’s next? You now have a repeatable, validated way to upgrade NetScaler from a single console. For the steps that come before and after the job itself, see the rest of our upgrade series:  How Do I: Perform zero-downtime NetScaler upgrades using ISSU?  How Do I: Validate a NetScaler upgrade and confirm it succeeded?  Got stuck or hit something unexpected in your environment? Drop a comment and we'll help you work through it.   Official documentation NetScaler Console service: Upgrade jobs  NetScaler Console service documentation

Device names follow the name template when "Apply name template only to new devices" is off — The OU template applies at every check-in, and Scout Board applies it when an OU is moved. The option is on by default. Turned off, devices with non-matching names are renamed at their first check-in after the update.  Maximum file size applies to every Scout Board upload — Covers configuration import, labels, and files, and values of 0 or less are rejected. items.title: Zero Trust for MCP: Controlling what AI agents are allowed to do
items.summary: Most people use GenAI to answer questions. Add MCP, and the AI can start doing things. Model Context Protocol gives AI agents a relatively clean way to interact with enterprise systems. An MCP server can expose tools for reading information, creating objects, updating records, or invoking whatever backend operation an application decided to wrap in a tool. Once those tools are connected to an agent, we now need to determine which of them should be available to the person behind the request.  Consider an MCP server exposing 42 customer-management tools. A financial analyst might legitimately need to read customer information and modify customer records. Someone on the support desk needs some of the same information but has no reason to create, update, or delete anything. Both people are authenticated and both can use the server, but they need very different privileges once they get there. Giving both of them all 42 tools because the connector authenticated successfully would be convenient, but unfortunately "the connection worked" is a fairly poor authorization policy.  Zero trust for applications already has a shape most of us know. The policy looks at who the user is, where they are, and what device they're on, and then decides what they can reach. Citrix SecurAccess ZTNA applies that same kind of policy to MCP, except that the thing being granted is a set of tools instead of an application.    Building the policy Setup happens once per server. An administrator adds the MCP server in the SecurAccess console, whether it sits on the public internet or inside the corporate network, and gets back a gateway URL. The AI platform is pointed at that URL instead of the server's own address, which puts the SecurAccess gateway in the path of every request.  Discovery is what makes policy creation possible. The administrator authorizes SecurAccess to sign in to the server, using a client ID and secret registered with the server's own identity provider, and SecurAccess asks the server what it offers. The result is a catalog of tools that are the basis for the SecurAccess policy rules. You might not be able to tell what a tool does from its name alone, so SecurAccess discovery categorizes each tool based on the action it performs: read, create, update, delete, or other. That categorization is what makes policy practical, because nobody wants to write rules against 42 individual tool names when selecting the category "read" will do.    With the catalog in place, a policy is scoped to an MCP server, and its rules grant tools to users or groups, optionally under conditions such as location and device posture. A rule can grant every tool or only a selection, by category or by individual tool.  Give an AI agent the same request under different user rolesTake a straightforward request: update the status for CompanyABC to production.    For the Finance group, the matching rule grants all 42 tools, including read, create, update, and delete operations. The update is within that group's capabilities and is authorized. Support reaches the same MCP server, but its matching rule grants ten read tools. Create, update, and delete aren't included.  Agents are eager to finish the job, and they tend to define the job more generously than we would. The support user's agent, being helpful in the way only software with no sense of consequences can be, tries the update anyway. The policy blocks the call, and the agent reports back with something close to this:  I attempted to update the status for CompanyABC. to production as you confirmed, but the action failed. The system returned an access denied by policy error. It appears you may not have required permissions to modify customer status in this connector.  That tells you where the control has to sit. The gateway evaluates each tool call as it arrives, so the outcome doesn't depend on what the agent decides to attempt, and a call it can't evaluate is denied.  The recorded demo walks through exactly this: the same request from the Finance and Support users, and the call that gets blocked. Watch the demo   When rules overlap A policy usually holds several rules, and one user can match more than one, because workers are routinely asked to do the jobs of several people at once. Take an analyst who also belongs to the support group. SecurAccess evaluates the rules from top to bottom in priority order, and the first match wins. Nothing below it is looked at.  So the order is part of the policy. Put the Finance support rule above the Finance analyst rule, and that analyst gets ten read tools, because evaluation stops at the support rule and never reaches the analyst one. Swap them, and the same person gets all 42. Both outcomes are exactly what the list says, which is the problem if nobody decided on purpose. For every pair of rules that can overlap, somebody has to pick the winner, and the winner goes higher.  Identity doesn't have to be the only context Years of zero trust taught us not to authorize on identity alone, a lesson that apparently needs repeating whenever a new protocol shows up. A SecurAccess MCP policy can bring location and device posture into the rule, which is how a rule tells a managed laptop from a personal one. A developer persona can have read-write access from a compliant device, support can have read-only access, and another persona can have no MCP tool access at all. Add a compliant-device condition to the developer rule and the same request is denied from a non-compliant device, then succeeds once the device becomes compliant.  The reason is the same as for any other application. Identity tells you who authenticated but says nothing about the conditions around them. A personal device may be unpatched or unmanaged, and a login from an unfamiliar location is what stolen credentials tend to look like. Agents raise the stakes, because an agent acts with the user's authority at machine speed. Someone acting maliciously used to need to understand where the data lived and how to get to it, which took time and left a trail. With an agent in the session they can describe what they want and let the AI do the finding, and a hijacked session on a weak endpoint can ask it to delete records as easily as read them. So the sensible response to higher-risk activities is to keep the user productive and take the dangerous tools off the table: reads stay available, and create, update and delete wait for a trusted device.  Finding out why a call failed A blocked call is only useful if somebody can work out why it was blocked. From the user's side of the chat window there's an agent apologizing about permissions, and that's about all there is to go on.  The administrator has more. Every decision the gateway makes becomes an event in Citrix Monitor, recording which MCP server and tool were involved, which policy was evaluated, and whether the call was allowed or blocked. "The AI couldn't update the customer" becomes a lookup. Was the tool in the rule? Did a stricter rule apply because of the device or location? The same events are worth reading when nothing failed, since a rule that grants more than anyone intended shows up as tools being called that nobody expected.  The governed path has to be the only path A policy only works if the request goes through the gateway. The MCP server still has its own address, and an agent that can reach it directly skips the policy entirely. So the deployment blocks the MCP server's direct address and leaves only the gateway's pathway open. Otherwise the policy only applies to agents willing to use the secure path, which are not the ones you're worried about.

items.title: Inside the sandbox -  how Citrix SecurSpaces runs enterprise agents
items.summary: AI agents are shifting from simple query-response assistants to active autonomous actors. Today, they routinely read raw files, execute terminal commands, and push code changes directly. For IT and security teams, this redefines the operational attack surface. The core governance challenge is no longer just what an agent is programmed to do - it’s what it can access in its environment. When an agent runs on a user’s endpoint, it inherits all the local permissions, tokens, and files accessible to that employee. That creates a wide radius of unintended exposure for autonomous software. Which brings us to a key architecture question: where should enterprise AI agents actually run? Moving beyond the endpoint: the case for sandboxing Most agent operations happen locally - reading files, refactoring code, maintaining context in memory, or invoking CLI tools. Because these actions occur entirely on the device, they don't generate the outbound network traffic that traditional gateways inspect. While a network gateway can monitor outbound API calls, it remains blind to an agent’s local file and system execution. On a standard endpoint, nothing ensures the agent consistently routes through security controls. This is where Citrix SecurSpaces changes the model. Instead of giving AI agents unrestricted access to local endpoints, it places them inside dedicated, governed workspaces. Each workspace provides only the tools, credentials, and access policies needed for the job - keeping all other enterprise assets secure by default. Instead of managing an unpredictable endpoint, security teams gain a predictable, isolated execution environment. Field-tested proof: secure developer workspaces AI coding tools already analyze repositories, run builds, and interface with internal staging systems daily. Development teams were among the first to validate this approach, using Citrix SecurSpaces to isolate AI tools without slowing down development momentum. Because these cloud-based environments connect seamlessly to browser IDEs, terminals, or local editors like VS Code and JetBrains via SSH, developers maintain full workflow flexibility: Containerized: Every workspace starts fresh from a verified base image. Developers and agents can build, test, and instantly reset to a clean state whenever needed. Standardized templates: Project leads define workspace templates once. New team members and AI tools launch identical environments in minutes, removing configuration drift and local environment friction. Governed network paths: All outbound traffic flows securely through the Citrix SecurSpaces proxy service by default. The result is rapid iteration and effortless setup, backed by automatic activity logging and workspace-level controls. Watch how Citrix development teams use Citrix SecurSpaces to slash environment setup times and safely build AI innovations like Citrix Adrian. Better together: execution + traffic flowCitrix SecurSpaces operates as an integrated component of the broader Citrix Platform. Complete agent governance relies on two complementary layers: Layer  What it controls Citrix products  Traffic Flow   Outbound requests, model queries, and MCP tool calls. Citrix NetScaler /  Citrix SecurAccess  Execution  Local file access, agent activity, credentials, and tool runtime. Citrix SecurSpaces  Relying on traffic flow control alone leaves a gap - AI gateways can only enforce policies on traffic they receive. When agents execute inside a Citrix SecurSpaces workspace, outbound routing is enforced at the OS and container level. Model and MCP calls automatically pass through your designated AI gateway (such as NetScaler AI Gateway) for full inspection and policy enforcement. Bringing the same protection to business teams Software engineers proved the sandboxed execution model, but the need for governance isn't limited to developer tools. To bring these same guardrails to business operations, Citrix is releasing the Knowledge Worker Agent for Citrix SecurSpaces as an open-source project under the Apache License 2.0. This conversational assistant lets non-technical teams analyze documents, run multi-step workflows, and safely interact with enterprise applications. Because the Knowledge Worker Agent executes inside a SecurSpaces sandbox, IT retains full control over which models, enterprise tools, and data repositories the agent can touch. Finance, legal, HR, and procurement teams get the exact same enterprise-grade execution security that developers rely on daily. Learn more: Your users already use AI agents: give them a safe place to run Wrapping up Endpoints aren't designed to safely host autonomous execution tools. Running unmonitored agents on local machines introduces unnecessary enterprise security risk. By hosting AI execution within governed, sandboxed workspaces, organizations deliver the ideal balance: maximum productivity for business teams and zero-trust confidence for IT. Ready to try it? Deploy your first environment today with the Citrix SecurSpaces Community Edition on Azure Marketplace. Migrate one ungoverned agent task to a secure workspace and experience the control and visibility firsthand.
